quotes.text: Access controls determine which data can be retrieved, prompt injection determines how that data is interpreted, and how the model behaves once it sees that data.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Draws the key line between permissions and model behavior that most Copilot security reviews miss.

quotes.text: Your system prompt isn't a security boundary. It is a string of text that competes with every other string of text in the context window for the model's attention.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Debunks the common belief that system instructions act as a firewall.

quotes.text: You can't patch this vulnerability with a software update. You can't fix it with a firewall rule. You must change the architecture.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Frames indirect prompt injection as a structural design problem rather than a bug.

quotes.text: Dual LLM verification makes the poison harmless by ensuring that raw retrieved content never reaches a model that has the power to act on it.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Summarizes the core idea of the recommended architectural defense.

quotes.text: Your co-pilot doesn't create new data risks. It exposes the ones you already have. The difference between a pilot and a breach is whether you assume trust or verify it.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A concise closing thesis linking Copilot risk to existing data hygiene and zero trust.

takeaways: In RAG-based copilots every retrieved document becomes part of the prompt, so hidden text in SharePoint, email or Teams content can act as instructions.
Access controls and system prompts do not stop indirect prompt injection; defenses must be architectural, such as dual LLM verification with a non-LLM controller.
Zero-trust prompting, continuous red teaming and basic data hygiene of the retrieval corpus are needed before scaling Copilot beyond pilots.
hook: Your Microsoft 365 Copilot reads SharePoint pages, emails and Teams chats that may hide instructions an attacker planted there. This episode explains for security and IT leaders why indirect prompt injection is an architectural flaw of RAG and how red teaming, dual LLM verification and zero-trust prompting close the gap.
